Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement

Is PRP Safe? Risks, Quality and Standards

Because PRP uses your own blood, people often assume it is risk-free. It is still an injection procedure.

Home/Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement/PRP and Breast Enhancement/Is PRP Safe? Risks, Quality and Standards

Because PRP uses your own blood, people often assume it is risk-free. It is lower risk than some products in terms of allergy, but it is still an injection procedure. This page is part of our guide to PRP and breast enhancement.

Possible risks

  • Pain, bruising and swelling at the injection site
  • Infection, particularly if sterile technique is poor
  • Bleeding
  • Lumps or nodules
  • Skin irritation or changes in pigment
  • Nerve irritation
  • Contamination of the preparation, if handled incorrectly
  • Cross-contamination if equipment or blood samples are mixed up

Who may need extra care

People with bleeding or platelet disorders, active infection, blood cancers, those on blood thinners, and pregnant or breastfeeding people should talk to their doctor before PRP.

Quality and standards

A safe clinic will:

  • Use single-use, sterile kits designed for the purpose
  • Follow clear labelling and identification of your blood sample
  • Have trained staff and a medical setting
  • Explain the preparation method and its limits
  • Provide written information and obtain consent

Imaging

PRP itself is not known to cause lasting changes on mammograms, but any injected treatment should be mentioned to imaging teams.

Costs

PRP is often sold in packages of sessions. Ask about the evidence for repeated treatment before paying in advance. See breast enlargement safety for wider checks.

Questions to ask

  • How is the sample handled and labelled?
  • What are the risks specific to breast injections?
  • What happens if I have a complication?

Know when to seek help

Fever, spreading redness, increasing pain, discharge, severe swelling or changing skin colour need prompt medical advice. Keep the procedure record, including the date and site, so an imaging or emergency team has accurate information.

Using your own blood may reduce some allergy concerns, but sterility, correct labelling, injection skill and an appropriate clinical setting remain essential. A new breast symptom should still be assessed rather than assumed to be a harmless procedure effect.

Key takeaway

"Your own blood" does not mean no risk. Look for medical standards and honest explanations.
